name: Church organization as political pressure group
plain_explanation: Before Constantine, Christians built a tightly organized, disciplined community (with bishops, charity networks, and shared doctrine) that functioned, in effect, like a unified voting bloc or pressure group in a world where no other group was organized in the same way.
precise_definition: The 'union and discipline of the Christian republic' (Gibbon's fifth cause): the distinctive organizational cohesion of the Christian community -- centered on episcopal authority, reinforced by control of charitable almsgiving -- which gave Christians disproportionate collective political leverage even as a minority.
why_it_mattered: Russell regards this, more than Gibbon does, as probably the single most important political cause of Christianity's success and of Constantine's calculated favor toward it.
historical_origin: Developed gradually through the first three centuries, accelerating after Constantine's conversion when bishops acquired judicial and administrative power.
examples: Bishops' control of alms to the poor creating a loyal urban following
The Council of Nicaea as an early instance of centralized doctrinal authority
competing_positions: Gibbon's own ranking, which places this cause last rather than first in importance
influence_on_later_thinkers: Analogous, Russell notes, to the modern political power of an organized voting bloc (e.g., the 'Catholic vote').
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly political: explains Constantine's strategic calculation in favoring Christianity.
